title: Of Course They're Using AI! Why Wouldn't They?
author: Dempsey, Patrick
summary: Patrick Dempsey opens a series on motivation and flow by targeting what he argues is the foundational incoherence of institutional education: we expect students to be maximally engaged at externally assigned times—50 minutes on Monday, 50 on Wednesday, 50 on Friday—and then express bafflement when they reach for AI to complete work they never chose. The system was designed not around the conditions of learning but around the institution's need to coordinate time and space, and those constraints have been inherited without critical examination at every level, from the student schedule to the AI committee that meets every other Thursday. Genuine learning and creative work require room to stay with a problem—periods of apparent inactivity, moments of insight, iterative experimentation, self-evidencing feedback—none of which survive constant interruption or calendar control. The essay closes by framing the series ahead: an exploration of flow and deep engagement as the alternative logic that education has never fully adopted.
points: Students are expected to be maximally motivated at externally assigned times across 40+ courses over 4 years—an expectation with no basis in how motivation or learning actually works.
The current education structure was designed around the institution's need to coordinate time and space, not around the conditions under which genuine learning occurs.

AI use by students is a rational response to a system that assigns work disconnected from intrinsic motivation—moral outrage at AI shortcuts misdiagnoses the design failure as a student character failure.
Creating new knowledge, ideas, or ways of working requires uninterrupted room to stay with a problem through periods of apparent stagnation—none of which education's fragmented schedule allows.

The same structural problem operates at the institutional level: an AI committee that meets 60 minutes every other Thursday cannot be expected to generate anything beyond what the institution already has.
quotes: We give students subjects in small, intermittent doses: fifty minutes on Monday, fifty minutes on Wednesday, fifty minutes on Friday. We pick the time, the place, and the topic.
We legitimately wonder why they would use AI to do their work? We even get indignant when they do!
Fundamentally, higher education is designed around the institution’s need to coordinate time and space. Hard stop.
The AI-committee that meets for 60 minutes every other Thursday. What exactly do we expect they’ll be able to do??? Are we really expecting something exceptional from them?
Creating something new—new knowledge, new ideas, new inspiration, new ways of working—requires room to stay with a problem. It requires periods when very little appears to be happening
None of that arrives according to a calendar, and it cannot survive constant interruption.
We have built education—and the work we do around it—on the assumption that learning and creating can be divided, assigned, and controlled.
